channel.description: Recent content in Contracts on Best of AI

item.title: ArborGold
item.description:
Arborists can build quotes from price lists, schedule crews, and send invoices from the field. Mobile apps let crews see jobs and update status. Customer history helps with repeat work and follow-ups.

It is aimed at small and mid-size companies. Features are practical rather than AI heavy.

Jobber and Housecall Pro are broader field service alternatives. ArborGold suits tree care businesses.

item.title: Floranext
item.description:
Designers take phone and web orders, print tickets, and schedule deliveries. Customer records track occasions for reminders. Online stores are built into the system.

It is a subscription product for flower shops.

Lightspeed and Shopify can work with extra setup. Floranext suits floral designers who run a shop.

item.title: Fresha
item.description:
Salons manage calendars, take payments, and send reminders. Clients find and book services on a marketplace. Reports track sales and staff performance.

The software is free to start, with fees on payments and some features.

Vagaro and StyleSeat are alternatives. Fresha suits cosmetologists and salon owners.

item.title: MassageBook
item.description:
Clients book and fill out intake forms online. Therapists record notes after each session and send reminders. A free plan covers basics, and paid plans add marketing tools.

It is built for solo practitioners and small clinics.

Vagaro and Jane are alternatives. MassageBook suits massage therapists.

item.title: Mindbody
item.description:
Studios set up classes, accept bookings, and manage memberships. Clients book through a branded app or the Mindbody marketplace. Reporting and marketing tools support growth, and AI features help with messaging.

It is a subscription product with tiered pricing.

Vagaro and Zen Planner are alternatives. Mindbody suits yoga instructors who run a studio.

item.title: MoeGo
item.description:
Groomers see appointments by staff and van, store pet profiles, and send reminders. Customers book online and pay by card. AI answers calls and messages in some plans.

It is a subscription product.

Gingr and Pawfinity are alternatives. MoeGo suits pet groomers and small pet service shops.

item.title: Passare
item.description:
Directors build arrangements, collect e-signatures, and share planning details with families. Obituary and tribute tools help families write remembrances. Reports track revenue and pre-need contracts.

It is a subscription product for funeral homes.

FrontRunner and Osiris are alternatives. Passare suits funeral directors.

item.title: Shopmonkey
item.description:
Technicians and service advisors build estimates from labor guides and parts catalogs, send them to customers for approval, and track the job through completion. Digital vehicle inspections with photos help explain recommended work. Text messaging keeps customers informed.

Shops use it to replace paper tickets and spreadsheets. Parts ordering and accounting integrations vary by plan.

Tekmetric and Shop-Ware are close alternatives. Shopmonkey suits independent repair shops.

item.title: Tekmetric
item.description:
Service advisors write estimates, send digital inspections with photos, and collect approval and payment by text or email. Reports show car count, average repair order, and technician productivity. Integrations connect to parts suppliers and accounting software.

Shops use the data to see what is working and where jobs stall. It is a subscription product with per-shop pricing.

Shopmonkey and Shop-Ware are alternatives. Tekmetric suits independent shop owners and managers.

item.title: Zen Planner
item.description:
Owners set up class schedules and membership plans, and members check in with an app or kiosk. Automated billing reduces missed payments. Reports show attendance and retention.

It is a subscription product.

Mindbody and Kicksite are alternatives. Zen Planner suits martial arts instructors who run a school.

item.title: Clio
item.description:
Clio is a practice management system for small and mid-sized law firms. It keeps matters, contacts, documents, calendars, and communications in one place, tracks billable time, produces invoices, and takes payments through trust accounting and online billing. Client intake tools capture new inquiries and conflict checks, and a client portal lets clients view documents and messages securely. For many firms, it replaces a patchwork of spreadsheets and separate apps.

The AI assistant, Clio Duo, helps with the paperwork. It can summarize a matter’s documents and emails, answer questions about a case, draft correspondence, and suggest time entries. Clio has also moved into legal research and drafting by acquiring a legal research company, adding tools to find authorities and prepare documents inside the same environment. These tools aim to reduce the time lawyers spend on administrative work and first drafts.

item.title: DISCO
item.description:
DISCO helps legal teams handle the huge volumes of documents produced in lawsuits and investigations. Teams upload email, files, and chats, search and tag them, and decide what is relevant and privileged. The platform runs in the cloud, so reviewers can work together without managing servers.

AI features reduce manual review. Models rank documents by likely relevance, so reviewers see the important ones first, and generative tools summarize documents, answer questions about a set, and help build timelines. Law firms and corporate legal departments use it to cut review costs and speed up cases.

item.title: Dropbox Sign
item.description:
Dropbox Sign lets people sign documents without printing them. You upload a file, mark where each signer needs to sign or fill in fields, and send it by email. Signers open it on any device, sign, and the finished copy is stored with an audit trail that shows who signed and when. Templates make repeat documents such as contracts and NDAs quick to send.

The product started as HelloSign and was acquired by Dropbox, which renamed it. It connects with Dropbox storage, Google Drive, Gmail, Microsoft tools, and CRM systems, so documents can be sent from where they already live. A developer API lets software companies embed signing flows inside their own products, and Dropbox has added AI features in its wider document tools.

item.title: Filevine
item.description:
Filevine began in personal injury practice and has expanded to many types of law. It gives a firm a single place to track each matter: documents, notes, deadlines, tasks, communications, and billing. Workflows can be customized so that each case type follows the steps a firm wants, with automations that assign tasks and send reminders.

AI features help with the paper-heavy parts of legal work. They can summarize medical records and long case files, draft demand letters and other documents from case data, and help respond to clients. A document review tool extracts key facts and organizes them, which saves paralegals hours on cases with large volumes of material. Client-facing portals and text messaging keep people informed.

item.title: HoneyBook
item.description:
HoneyBook is designed for people who sell services, such as photographers, designers, coaches, and consultants. A client inquiry arrives through a form, the owner sends a proposal with a contract and an invoice, and the client signs and pays online, all within a single flow. This replaces a patchwork of documents, email threads, and payment apps.

Other features support day-to-day work. Automations send reminders and follow-ups, a scheduler lets clients book meetings, and a client portal keeps messages, files, and payments in one timeline. Templates for proposals and questionnaires make repeat work faster, and AI helps draft emails and project descriptions. Reports show income and pipeline.

item.title: Housecall Pro
item.description:
Housecall Pro helps small service companies run their operations. Office staff schedule jobs and dispatch technicians on a calendar and map, customers receive confirmations and arrival notifications, and technicians use a mobile app to see their jobs, send estimates, collect signatures, and take payments on site. Invoices and payments flow into accounting.

The platform includes marketing and sales tools. Review requests, email campaigns, and a customer database help a business grow repeat work, and a booking widget lets homeowners schedule online. Some AI features answer calls and messages, help with scheduling and follow-ups, and summarize job details so owners can stay on top of the business.

item.title: LegalOn
item.description:
LegalOn helps legal teams review contracts faster. A lawyer opens a draft in Word, and the tool checks it against a review checklist, highlighting risky or missing clauses and suggesting alternative wording. The checklists are built by lawyers, which the company says makes the guidance reliable.

Beyond review, the platform offers features for contract creation and management, and AI that answers questions about legal matters and compares language across documents. It started in Japan under the name LegalForce, where it grew quickly, and has expanded into North America and Europe.

item.title: LegalZoom
item.description:
LegalZoom helps people handle common legal tasks without a law firm. Users answer questions online, and the service prepares and files documents for things like forming an LLC or corporation, creating wills and trusts, registering trademarks and copyrights, and handling name changes. Registered agent services, compliance filings, and business licenses are available for new companies.

Human help is available at higher levels. Plans can include attorney consultations, document review, and legal advice subscriptions, and some tasks are reviewed by staff before filing. The company has added AI tools to guide users through forms, answer questions, and speed up document preparation, though legal advice itself comes from licensed professionals.

item.title: Legora
item.description:
Legora is a legal AI company from Sweden that has expanded globally. Lawyers use its assistant for tasks such as reviewing contracts and extracting key terms across many documents, researching legal questions, summarizing materials, and drafting and revising documents. A Word add-in brings these abilities into the editor where lawyers already work, so suggestions appear as tracked changes.

The platform emphasizes collaboration and structure. Features such as tabular review let teams compare many documents side by side in a grid, workflows capture a firm’s preferred processes, and shared workspaces allow lawyers and clients to work together. Firms can customize the system with their own playbooks and precedents, and security features aim to meet the confidentiality needs of legal practice.

item.title: LexisNexis Protégé
item.description:
Protégé is the AI layer of LexisNexis’s legal research platform. Lawyers can ask research questions in plain language and receive answers that cite cases, statutes, and secondary sources from the LexisNexis collection, with links to the underlying authorities. It can summarize documents, compare them, extract key terms, and draft memos and clauses, and it connects with the Shepard’s citation service to help check whether authorities are still good law.

Newer versions emphasize agentic work and the lawyer’s workflow. Protégé can break a task into steps, such as gathering documents, researching issues, and producing a draft, and works in Microsoft Word so suggestions appear in the document being edited. Firms can customize it with their own documents and playbooks, and security terms are designed for confidential client information.

item.title: Rocket Lawyer
item.description:
Rocket Lawyer is aimed at people who need legal help without a full law firm engagement. Members answer questions in an interview format and the service generates documents such as lease agreements, NDAs, wills, and operating agreements. Documents can be signed electronically and stored, and templates are tailored to the user’s state.

Beyond documents, membership gives access to attorneys through ask-a-lawyer services and, for some matters, discounted consultations. Small businesses use it for formation, contracts, and compliance support. AI tools help explain legal terms and draft documents, and are positioned as a way to get started before consulting a professional.

item.title: Teachable
item.description:
Teachable is a platform for people who want to sell what they know. A creator uploads video lessons, text, and quizzes, organizes them into a course, sets a price, and publishes it on a branded school site. Students enroll, pay, and track their progress, and the creator gets sales and engagement data.

The platform handles the business side. It processes payments in many currencies, supports subscriptions, bundles, and coupons, and offers tools for affiliate programs and email marketing. Coaching products and downloadable files can be sold alongside courses, and certificates reward completion. AI features help draft course outlines and descriptions.

item.title: Thinkific
item.description:
Thinkific is an online course platform. Creators build courses from video, audio, text, and quizzes, organize them into chapters, and host them on a site with their own branding and domain. Students log in to learn, and the platform tracks completion and issues certificates.

Features extend beyond courses. Memberships and communities keep learners engaged, bundles and subscriptions provide pricing options, and integrations connect with email tools, payment processors, and Zapier. Businesses also use Thinkific to train customers, partners, and employees, and AI tools help generate course outlines and quiz questions.

item.title: Boundless
item.description:
Boundless helps people navigate US immigration paperwork. Users answer questions in a guided flow, and the software builds the forms needed for a case, such as a marriage-based green card or naturalization. Checks flag missing information and inconsistencies that often cause delays.

Human experts remain part of the process. Plans include review by immigration attorneys or specialists, and customers can get help with responding to requests from authorities. Tracking tools show deadlines and the status of the case, and educational material explains steps and timelines.

item.title: Docketwise
item.description:
Docketwise is built specifically for immigration law. Attorneys collect information from clients with online questionnaires, and the software places answers on the correct government forms, which saves repeated typing. Because forms change, the platform keeps them updated.

It manages the rest of a case. Deadlines and receipts are tracked, status updates can be pulled from government sources, and client portals let people upload documents and see progress. Billing and email integrations support daily practice, and AI features help with drafting and summarizing.

item.title: Everlaw
item.description:
Everlaw helps legal teams work through evidence. Documents are uploaded, processed, and made searchable, and reviewers tag them, share notes, and build case narratives. Visual tools show relationships and timelines, and cloud delivery means teams can collaborate without installing software.

AI speeds up the work. Predictive coding ranks documents by likely relevance, clustering groups similar content, and generative features summarize documents, answer questions across a set, and draft deposition outlines. Everlaw has tools used by public interest lawyers and human rights investigators, and the company supports access programs.

item.title: Jobber
item.description:
Jobber is built for small service companies such as lawn care, cleaning, plumbing, and locksmith businesses. Owners send quotes, schedule jobs on a calendar, dispatch crews, and invoice customers, with a mobile app for the crew to see their route, take notes, and collect payment on site.

Client-facing features help win and keep work. Customers can request services online, approve quotes, pay invoices, and receive reminders and arrival notices, and a client hub keeps their history together. Automations send follow-ups and review requests. An AI assistant drafts messages and helps convert rough notes into a clear quote.

item.title: Kajabi
item.description:
Kajabi is an all-in-one platform for knowledge businesses. A creator builds a site, sells courses, memberships, coaching, and digital downloads, collects payments, runs email campaigns, and hosts a community, all from one dashboard instead of stitching together several tools.

Marketing and automation are built in. Landing pages, funnels, email sequences, and a pipeline for leads let creators sell without extra software. The AI assistant helps write copy, plan courses, and generate emails, and analytics show revenue and engagement. Mobile apps for members are available.

item.title: Noterro
item.description:
Noterro is built for small bodywork and rehab practices. Clients book online and fill in intake forms before arriving, and therapists record sessions with notes. An AI feature turns a few prompts into a structured SOAP note, saving time at the end of each appointment.

Other tools cover everyday needs: scheduling, reminders, payments, packages and memberships, and insurance claims where relevant. Reports track revenue and client retention.

Noterro is paid, with plans per practitioner. It is aimed at solo practitioners and small clinics. Alternatives include Jane, Cliniko, MassageBook, Vagaro, and SimplePractice. Noterro suits manual therapists who want simpler admin.

item.title: SimplePractice
item.description:
SimplePractice is widely used by solo and small group private practices. Clients book appointments online, complete intake forms in a portal, and join video sessions, while clinicians keep notes, treatment plans, and billing in the same system. Insurance claims can be submitted electronically.

AI features help clinicians write progress notes from session details and speed up documentation, which is a chief burden for therapists. The platform offers reminders, reporting, and a client app for messaging and payments.

item.title: StyleSeat
item.description:
StyleSeat serves independent beauty professionals. Clients search for stylists, browse portfolios and reviews, and book appointments, while professionals manage their calendar, take deposits, and process payments through the platform.

The marketplace helps new clients find providers, and the business tools handle reminders, no-show protection, and client records. Recommendations use location and preference data to match clients.

StyleSeat has a subscription for professionals and fees on some transactions. Fees for marketplace clients can be a concern for stylists with an existing following. Alternatives include Vagaro, Fresha, Booksy, Square Appointments, and Glossgenius. StyleSeat suits independent stylists and barbers.

item.title: Vagaro
item.description:
Vagaro runs the front desk for beauty and wellness businesses. Clients book online or through a marketplace app, staff manage calendars, take payments, and track inventory. Reminders and no-show protection reduce lost appointments.

Marketing tools include email and text campaigns, loyalty programs, and a presence on the Vagaro marketplace. AI answers calls and messages, helps book appointments, and suggests promotions.

Vagaro charges a monthly fee per business, with add-ons and payment processing fees. Alternatives include Fresha, Booksy, StyleSeat, Square Appointments, and Mindbody. Vagaro suits salons, spas, and studios.

item.title: Lettu
item.description:
Lettu is a platform for brands, agencies, and creators who work together. Influencer and creator campaigns involve briefs, contracts, approvals, payments, and usage rights, which are often handled in scattered emails. Lettu puts these into one workflow with legal templates drafted by lawyers.

The platform helps brands and agencies draft briefs, agree terms, track deliverables, and manage rights, such as how long content can be used. It draws on the law firm’s experience in advertising and media law, and AI features speed up drafting and review.

item.title: Astra for Law
item.description:
Astra for Law packages OpenAI’s model for legal work. Rather than a separate model, it pairs a general model with a dedicated search index of U.S. case law, statutes, regulations, and court rules, and instructions shaped for legal analysis and drafting. The goal is research answers that are grounded in sources a lawyer can check.

Access has been limited. OpenAI offered it first to selected firms through a trusted access program, with plans to make it available to legal technology companies through the API so they can build it into their own products. Partner plugins connect it to tools used in legal practice, such as document review, practice management, and document management systems.

item.title: Born to Found
item.description:
Born to Found guides first-time founders through the early journey. It divides company building into stages, such as validating an idea, building a first product, and finding customers, and supplies playbooks and checklists for each, so a founder knows what to focus on at their point.

An AI coach answers questions and reviews work, drawing on the founder’s stage and project details. This offers a low-cost alternative to mentors for people who lack access to experienced advisors, and a structure to keep going when the path is unclear.

item.title: C3.ai
item.description:
C3.ai builds packaged AI applications and a platform for developing them. Instead of starting from scratch, a company can adopt an application for a defined problem, such as predicting when equipment will fail, detecting fraud, or optimizing inventory, and connect it to their data. The platform provides tools for data integration, modeling, and deployment.

The company has moved to add generative AI. Its offerings include tools that let users ask questions about enterprise data in natural language and agent features for business workflows. Customers include utilities, manufacturers, banks, and defense and government agencies, where large-scale deployments are common.

item.title: Bonsai
item.description:
Bonsai bundles the paperwork of independent work. A freelancer sends a proposal, converts it into a contract with e-signature, tracks time or milestones, sends an invoice, and receives payment. A client portal keeps everything in one place, which helps a one-person business look established.

Additional tools cover running the business. Expense tracking, tax estimates, and banking features support finances, and workflow automations send reminders for unpaid invoices. AI helps draft contract language and project descriptions. Templates are available for design, consulting, development, and other fields.

item.title: Relativity
item.description:
Relativity is a leading e-discovery platform. Legal teams load documents collected in a case, and the system processes them, makes them searchable, and lets reviewers tag and code them for relevance, privilege, and confidentiality. RelativityOne runs in the cloud.

AI helps lawyers cut review volume. Active learning ranks documents by likely relevance, clustering groups similar items, and generative features summarize documents and find key evidence. Analytics show patterns in communications, and audit trails support defensible processes.

item.title: ServiceTitan
item.description:
ServiceTitan is built for home service trades. Call center staff book jobs, dispatchers assign technicians, technicians use a mobile app to quote and invoice with good-better-best pricing, and the office tracks job costs, marketing, and payroll. Everything ties to one customer record.

Data and AI help companies grow. Tools score inbound calls, flag missed opportunities, recommend pricing, and predict technician performance, and agents assist with booking and follow-ups. Reporting shows revenue per technician and marketing return.

item.title: Trust & Will
item.description:
Trust & Will makes estate planning approachable. A user answers questions about family, assets, and wishes, and the platform produces documents tailored to their state’s law. Plans can include wills, revocable trusts, powers of attorney, and healthcare directives.

Legal review options and notarization help make documents valid, and the service stores them securely. Price is usually lower than a full attorney engagement, which draws people who have put off planning.

item.title: Casetext
item.description: Casetext began as a community site where lawyers annotated and shared case law, then grew into a legal research service with tools such as a brief-checking feature called Parallel Search, which found relevant cases using natural language. It was among the first legal technology companies to build on large language models, and its CoCounsel assistant could review documents, summarize depositions, draft research memos, and help prepare contract analyses with citations to sources.

item.title: DocuSign AI
item.description:
Docusign made electronic signatures routine. Senders upload a document, specify signers and fields, and recipients sign on any device, with an audit trail and legal validity in many countries. It’s used for sales contracts, HR paperwork, real estate, and any agreement that once needed a pen, and it integrates with Salesforce, Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, and many business systems.

The company has expanded to manage the whole agreement lifecycle. Its Intelligent Agreement Management platform includes tools to prepare and negotiate agreements, a repository that stores them, and AI that reads contracts to extract terms such as renewal dates, obligations, and parties. Its AI can summarize documents, answer questions about a contract portfolio, and flag risks, and workflow tools automate steps such as approvals and routing.

item.title: DoNotPay
item.description:
DoNotPay started by helping people contest parking tickets and grew into an app for dealing with the small annoyances of consumer life. Its tools help users write letters and fill out forms to dispute charges, cancel unwanted subscriptions, request refunds, and complain to companies and agencies. The idea is that many of these tasks are tedious and intimidating, and a template-driven assistant can save people time and money.

The company’s marketing as the world’s first robot lawyer caused trouble. The Federal Trade Commission alleged that the service did not perform as well as a human lawyer and did not have the testing to back its claims. A final order barred DoNotPay from making that kind of claim without evidence and required it to pay a fine and notify affected customers. The case is often cited as a warning about overstating what AI can do in legal matters.

item.title: Harvey
item.description:
Harvey was built for lawyers and has become one of the best-known legal AI companies. Attorneys use its assistant to ask legal questions, draft and revise contracts and memos, summarize documents, and analyze large sets of files, such as the documents in a due diligence review. It runs on leading language models adapted for legal work and is designed to provide citations so lawyers can verify the answers.

Beyond a chat assistant, Harvey offers structured features. Vault stores and analyzes large document collections, workflows automate multi-step tasks such as contract review against a playbook, and integrations connect with tools law firms already use, including document management and legal research providers. Firms can customize the system with their own templates and precedents, and security controls support the confidentiality requirements of legal practice.

item.title: HubSpot
item.description: HubSpot started as a marketing software company and grew into a full platform for managing the customer relationship from first visit to renewal. It is organized into hubs: Marketing Hub for email, forms, ads, and landing pages, Sales Hub for pipelines and sequences, Service Hub for tickets and help desk, Content Hub for websites and blogs, and Operations Hub for data syncing and automation. All of them read from the same CRM, so a marketer, a sales rep, and a support agent are looking at one record of the customer.

item.title: Ironclad
item.description:
Ironclad serves legal and business teams that handle many contracts. Requests start from templates through a workflow, drafts are negotiated with counterparties inside the platform, and approvals and e-signatures finish the process. Executed contracts become structured data in a repository.

AI features are central. They read incoming contracts, flag deviations from company positions, suggest edits, and extract key terms such as renewal dates and liability caps. A repository search lets teams answer questions about their agreements, and reports show where contracts get stuck.

item.title: Juro
item.description:
Juro puts the contract workflow in a browser editor. Sales and business teams generate contracts from approved templates, negotiate with counterparties in the same document, collect signatures, and store the result in a searchable repository. Legal sets the rules and approvals, so routine deals move without a lawyer.

AI is part of the product. It can draft clauses from a plain-English description, review third-party paper against a company’s positions, summarize agreements, and answer questions about the contract portfolio. Integrations with CRMs and messaging tools keep the process connected to sales.

item.title: Kira Systems
item.description:
Kira was one of the first widely adopted machine learning tools in legal work. It reads contracts and identifies provisions such as change of control, termination rights, assignment, and indemnification, then extracts the relevant text into a structured summary. Lawyers use it in mergers and acquisitions due diligence, where hundreds or thousands of agreements must be reviewed quickly, and in lease, finance, and compliance reviews.

Litera acquired Kira Systems and continues to develop it. The newer version adds generative AI to the original extraction models, with features like rapid clause analysis that organizes clauses across many documents. Users can start from built-in models for common provisions, train their own for specific needs, and review results in a side-by-side view that links back to the source text. Integration with Litera’s other tools connects review to drafting and transaction workflows.

item.title: LawGeex
item.description:
LawGeex addresses the high volume of routine contracts that reach legal departments, such as NDAs and standard vendor agreements. Legal teams define a playbook that states what is acceptable in each type of clause, and LawGeex’s AI reads incoming contracts and checks them against it. Contracts that conform can be approved quickly, and those that deviate are flagged with the problem and suggested edits.

The idea is to let lawyers focus on contracts that really need judgment. Business users can submit documents for review through integrations and workflows, and reviewers see a clear summary of what matched, what did not, and where to look. The system learns from corrections, and reporting shows how many contracts were reviewed and how long approvals take. It supports a range of commercial agreements.

item.title: Lexion
item.description:
Lexion helped legal teams make sense of their contracts. It read agreements, pulled out terms like parties, dates, renewal windows, and liability caps, and stored them in a searchable repository. Alerts warned teams about upcoming renewals and obligations, and workflows routed new requests.

AI answered questions across the portfolio, such as which contracts have auto-renewal or a particular clause. The company was built for fast-growing technology companies that wanted contract management without a heavy implementation.

item.title: Luminance
item.description:
Luminance is built for lawyers who deal with large volumes of agreements. Teams upload contracts, and the platform identifies key terms, highlights unusual or risky clauses, and compares documents against company standards. Its origins lie in machine learning developed at the University of Cambridge.

Beyond review, Luminance supports negotiation and drafting. An AI assistant can propose edits in Word, summarize positions, and handle routine agreements with limited human involvement, escalating exceptions to lawyers. In due diligence, it speeds through thousands of documents to find issues across a deal’s data room.

item.title: MarketMan
item.description:
MarketMan is back-of-house software for food service. Operators record what they buy and use, build recipes with ingredient costs, and see the cost of each dish. When prices change or usage varies, the system flags it, helping managers protect margins.

Ordering and invoicing are handled in one place. Staff place orders with suppliers, receive deliveries, and match invoices to what arrived, which catches errors and short shipments. Forecasting tools predict how much to order based on sales history, and integrations connect with point of sale and accounting systems.

item.title: PandaDoc AI
item.description:
PandaDoc helps sales teams close deals faster. Users build proposals and quotes from templates in a drag-and-drop editor, add pricing tables with live calculations, embed videos and payment links, and send them to clients, who can review and sign electronically. Tracking shows when a document is opened and viewed, so reps know when to follow up.

Automation and integration make it practical for teams. It connects with CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot to populate documents with deal data and update records when documents are signed, offers approval workflows, content libraries, and a payment step. AI features help generate document content from a prompt, summarize contracts, suggest edits, and extract information, speeding up proposal creation.

item.title: Proposify
item.description:
Proposify helps agencies and service companies create and send proposals. Teams build templates with sections, pricing tables, and brand styling, assemble a proposal quickly, and send it to clients who can review, comment, and sign electronically. Notifications show when a proposal is opened.

AI features help with writing content and suggest improvements based on what has worked in past proposals. Analytics reveal how long clients spend on each section, informing follow-ups. Integrations connect with CRMs and billing.

item.title: Qwilr
item.description:
Qwilr replaces static PDF proposals with web pages. A seller builds a proposal from blocks, such as text, images, videos, pricing tables, and acceptance sections, and sends a link. Buyers can adjust options in a pricing table, and sign online, which shortens the path to closing.

Analytics show who viewed the page, how long they spent on each section, and when they came back, which guides follow-up. Templates keep branding consistent, and integrations push data into CRMs. AI drafts content from notes and suggests improvements.

item.title: Salesforce Einstein
item.description:
Einstein brought AI to Salesforce customers well before generative AI became popular. Predictive features score leads and opportunities, forecast revenue, recommend next best actions, and flag at-risk accounts, using each company’s own CRM data. Einstein Discovery finds patterns and suggests what drives outcomes, and bots and analytics features extend the same ideas to service and marketing.

With generative AI, Einstein has expanded to write emails, summarize records and cases, and generate service replies, grounded in customer data and protected by the Einstein Trust Layer, which masks sensitive information and prevents customer data from being used to train outside models. The conversational assistant evolved into Agentforce, which builds autonomous agents on the same foundation, so Einstein now refers to a mix of older predictive features and the generative AI infrastructure.

item.title: ServiceNow
item.description:
ServiceNow began as an IT service management tool and became a general workflow platform for large organizations. Employees and customers submit requests, such as a laptop problem, a payroll question, or a customer complaint, and the platform routes, tracks, and resolves them using defined workflows. Companies use it as a system of record and action across IT operations, HR, legal, security, and customer service.

AI is central to its current strategy. Now Assist adds generative AI to summarize cases, draft replies, and help agents find answers, and AI agents can take on tasks such as triaging incidents and fulfilling requests with minimal human intervention. The company acquired Moveworks, whose employee assistant is intended to become the front door to the platform, and offers tools to govern and monitor agents across the enterprise.

item.title: Square
item.description:
Square is known for its card readers and registers. A small business accepts payments in person, online, or by invoice, tracks inventory, and manages staff and payroll from a single account. Hardware ranges from a simple reader to full countertop systems.

Additional services include appointments, loyalty programs, marketing, and small business loans based on sales. AI assistance writes item descriptions, generates insights from sales data, and answers business questions.

Square charges processing fees per transaction and sells hardware, with paid software tiers for advanced features. It has a free plan for basic use. Alternatives include Toast for restaurants, Clover, Shopify POS, Stripe Terminal, and SumUp. Square suits small retail and food businesses.

item.title: Toast
item.description:
Toast serves the restaurant industry. Servers take orders on handheld devices, kitchen displays route tickets, guests pay at the table or online, and managers track sales, labor, and inventory. Online ordering, delivery integrations, and loyalty programs are part of the ecosystem.

Data and AI support operations. Sales forecasts help schedule staff, menu analytics show what sells, and assistants help write menu descriptions and answer business questions. Payroll and team management tools extend the suite.

item.title: Zoho
item.description:
Zoho builds a wide range of business applications on its own platform. Companies can use Zoho CRM for sales, Books for accounting, Desk for support, Projects for work tracking, Mail for email, People for HR, and dozens of other apps, many of which integrate with one another. Zoho One bundles the whole suite for a single per-user price.

Zia is the AI layer. It predicts which leads are likely to convert, detects anomalies in data, drafts replies, and answers questions in natural language, and Zoho has added a generative assistant and agents that can act across apps. The company also supports the option of running models on its own infrastructure for customers who want data kept in their region.

item.title: Evisort
item.description:
Evisort uses AI to understand contracts. It ingests agreements, identifies clauses and key terms such as renewal dates, payment terms, and liability limits, and stores them as structured data. Teams can search across thousands of contracts, instead of hunting through PDFs.

It supports the contract lifecycle: drafting from templates, negotiating, tracking obligations, and getting alerts before renewals. Reports show risk and spend across the portfolio. Generative AI helps review contracts against playbooks and suggests changes.

item.title: Litera
item.description:
Litera is known for products lawyers use daily. Its comparison software shows exactly what changed between document versions, a core need in contract negotiation, and drafting tools check formatting, cross-references, and defined terms. Other products handle transaction management and closing checklists.

Newer AI features help review documents, summarize them, and spot inconsistencies or risk. The company has combined many acquired products into a suite for law firms and corporate legal departments, and it integrates with Microsoft Word and document management systems.

item.title: Denovo
item.description:
Denovo aims to shorten the path from idea to launched business. A user describes what they want to start, and the platform helps produce a business plan, suggests names and branding, generates a website, and walks through setup tasks such as registering the company. Putting these steps in one tool reduces the number of services a beginner must find and learn.

The target is people who have never started a company, or who want to test a side project quickly. AI-generated plans and sites provide a starting point, and users still need to validate demand with real customers and check legal requirements in their location.

item.title: Robin AI
item.description:
Robin AI developed tools for lawyers who spend their days reading contracts. Its platform used language models trained on legal text to review agreements, flag risks, suggest edits to bring them in line with a company’s playbook, and answer questions about clauses. It worked in Microsoft Word and was used by in-house legal teams and law firms for routine commercial agreements such as NDAs, supplier contracts, and sales terms.

The company also combined software with a managed legal services offering, in which lawyers reviewed work and handled volume for clients. That mix aimed to deliver quick, reliable turnaround, with AI doing the first pass and humans checking. It gained attention for fast growth and for partnerships and funding in the legal AI boom.

item.title: Spellbook
item.description:
Spellbook was built to meet lawyers where they work: in Word. As you draft or review a contract, it suggests language, flags missing or risky terms, and proposes edits as tracked changes. You can ask it questions about a clause, have it compare a draft with your standard positions, or generate a first draft from a prompt, always inside the document you are working on.

Features extend to the review and negotiation steps. A library of benchmarks shows how a term compares to market standards, a playbook feature lets firms encode their preferred positions for checking contracts, and agent-style workflows can run multi-step tasks such as reviewing a set of agreements. It’s used by law firms and in-house teams, particularly for transactional work, and builds on leading language models with legal-specific prompts and data.
